presenceLabel: Mosopelea or Ofo village in this area
presenceNote: No source dates the Ohio home of the Mosopelea; the sources give an end, not a start (gone from Ohio by 1673; villages marked destroyed on Franquelin’s map of 1684, whose date is the map’s, not a year of settlement). The map therefore shows ‘before 1673’, then the lower Mississippi to 1784. Their Ohio home is disputed (Griffin 1942). Kentucky appears only in Swanton’s conjecture that they may have stopped at the mouth of the Cumberland River; no village is documented there, and nothing is drawn in Kentucky. Low confidence; medium for the later Mississippi and Louisiana places.
overlapNote: Shawnee (their name for the Ohio River is a shortened form of Mosopelea), Miami-Illinois speakers (Mosopeleacipi), Quapaw, Taensa, Tunica, Biloxi, Yazoo, Koroa and Natchez. Tutelo shares many words with Ofo (Wikipedia).
basis: One French map of 1684 (Franquelin) via Hanna and Wikipedia; Swanton’s Indian Tribes of North America; later colonial records of the Ofo in Mississippi and Louisiana. Griffin 1942 challenges the Ohio Valley evidence. Mostly tertiary web sources.

eras.label: before 1673 · Ohio River, between the Muskingum and Scioto (disputed)
eras.text: A French map by Franquelin, dated 1684, shows eight Mosopelea villages just north of the Ohio River between the Muskingum and Scioto rivers, marked ‘destroyed’; La Salle said Seneca-led Iroquois conquered them in the early 1670s (Wikipedia, citing Hanna). By 1673, the year French explorers found they had left Ohio, they had gone down to the Mississippi. Both 1673 and 1684 are dates of departure and of a map, not years they lived here; no start year is known. The tint is the five Ohio counties on the river between the two mouths: a general area, and disputed, since Griffin (1942) judges the evidence for an Ohio Valley home unsatisfactory.

eras.label: 1673–c.1699 · Down the Mississippi, then the Quapaw and Taensa
eras.text: By 1673 they had gone down to the Mississippi and settled on its west side below the mouth of the Ohio; later they stopped among the Quapaw, and before 1686 at least part had gone to the Taensa (Swanton). Swanton’s entry for Kentucky adds that they may have stopped briefly at the mouth of the Cumberland River on the way; that is a conjecture, and no village is documented. Not drawn: no county or site is given.

eras.label: c.1699–1784 · Yazoo River, Fort Rosalie, Pointe Coupee
eras.text: In 1699 Iberville’s party found the Ofogoula on the Yazoo River, Mississippi. They refused to join the Natchez revolt (1729), lived with the Tunica, and were near Fort Rosalie by 1739 and until after 1758; in 1784 a dozen or so were with the Tunica on the Mississippi 8 miles above Pointe Coupee, Louisiana (EBSCO; Swanton). They merged into the Tunica-Biloxi; the last Ofo speaker was recorded in 1908. The tints are Yazoo and Adams counties, Mississippi, and Pointe Coupee Parish, Louisiana: general areas.

Griffin (1942) disputes the evidence. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.

Yazoo and Adams counties, Mississippi, as whole counties: the Yazoo River (1699) and the Fort Rosalie (Natchez) country (1739–after 1758). Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.

Pointe Coupee Parish, Louisiana, as a whole parish: a dozen or so Ofo with the Tunica on the Mississippi 8 miles above Pointe Coupee in 1784. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.
Fort Rosalie, Natchez, Mississippi (Wikipedia 31.557, -91.410). The Ofo lived near the fort from 1739 until after 1758; the point is the fort, not an Ofo village.
